rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By proposing to send a gift and await the envoys, the queen settles on a course of action; this indicates she did not trust Solomon to accept it.
rows.anchor: حتى أعمل بما يقتضيه الحال وهذا ظاهر في أنها لم تثق بقبوله عليه السلام هديتها

rows.speaker: بلقيس
rows.claim: A report says she reasoned that a worldly king would be satisfied by wealth, whereas a prophet would not, and should be followed in his religion.
rows.anchor: وروي أنها قالت لقومها : إن كان ملكا دنيويا أرضاه المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadiyya names something offered as a gift, just as ʿaṭiyya names something given.
rows.anchor: والهدية اسم لما يهدي كالعطية اسم لما يعطى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-nāẓira is coordinated with mursalatu; bi-ma depends on yarjiʿ, and the clause whose object is awaited is the complement of nazar.
rows.anchor: النظر معلق والجملة في موضع المفعول به له

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī attached bi-ma to nāẓira, but al-Ālūsī calls this a grave error, following al-Baḥr.
rows.anchor: ووقع للحوفي أنه متعلق بناظرة وهو وهم فاحش كما في البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verified nominal clause signals that she is firmly resolved to follow her judgment, unmoved by anything that might divert or dissuade her.
rows.anchor: والجملة الاسمية الدالة على الثبات المصدرة بحرف التحقيق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the queen's gift consisted of one hundred male servants and one hundred female servants.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس أنها كانت مائة وصيف ومائة وصيفة

rows.speaker: وهب وغيره
rows.claim: Wahb and others describe five hundred girls dressed as boys and five hundred boys as girls, with jeweled mounts, gold and silver bricks, a jeweled crown, perfumes, and a box holding a pearl and a crooked-holed carnelian.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب وغيره : عمدت بلقيس إلى خمسمائة جارية

rows.speaker: وهب وغيره
rows.claim: The queen sent a wise noble with tests: identify the disguised sexes and box contents, drill the pearl straight, thread the stone without human or jinn help, and watch whether Solomon appeared angry or welcoming.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب وغيره : عمدت بلقيس إلى خمسمائة جارية

rows.speaker: وهب وغيره
rows.claim: On the envoys' approach, Solomon had a nine-farsakh gold-and-silver field prepared, assembled remarkable creatures and his subjects in ranks, and received the party with a welcoming face.
rows.anchor: وأمرهم بعمل ميدان مقدار تسع فراسخ

rows.speaker: وهب وغيره
rows.claim: Gabriel disclosed the box's pearl and stone; a termite bored the pearl and a white worm threaded the stone, each receiving trees or fruit as its provision, and Solomon distinguished boys from girls by how they washed.
rows.anchor: فجاء جبريل عليه السلام فأخبره بما فيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account adds a hereditary Himyarite royal staff and a cup to be filled with water from neither earth nor sky; Solomon identified the staff's base by dropping it and filled the cup with horse sweat.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنها أنفذت مع هداياها عصا كان يتوارثها ملوك حمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says these stories cannot be known to be true or false, though some details incline the heart toward judging them fabricated.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك أخبار لايدرى صحتها ولا كذبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording omits the sending of the gift: she sent it, and when it reached Solomon, he spoke. The alternative takes the subject of “came” as the queen sending it; the first is preferable.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف أي فارسلت الهدية فلما جاء

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads the verb in the plural, “when they came,” referring to the messengers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله ( فلما جاؤا ) أي المرسلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may be to the envoy while grammatically including the sender, or to the envoy and his party; al-Ālūsī prefers the former because it extends the rebuke to the queen and her people, in keeping with the singular return command.
rows.anchor: خطاب للرسول والمرسل تغليبا للحاضر على الغائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form of māl belittles the wealth offered.
rows.anchor: وتنكير ( مال ) للتحقير

rows.speaker: جمهور السبعة
rows.claim: Most of the seven readers pronounce two nūns in tamuddūnani; some also retain the speaker's yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ جمهور السبعة ( تمدونن ) بنونين وأثبت بعض الياء

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza assimilates the indicative nūn into the protective nūn and retains the first-person yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة بادغام نون الرفع في نون الوقاية

rows.speaker: المسيبي عن نافع
rows.claim: Al-Musayyibī from Nāfiʿ reads a single light nūn, with the protective nūn omitted; an alternative analysis omits the first nūn and assumes an unexpressed inflectional marker.
rows.anchor: وقرأ المسيبي عن نافع بنون واحدة خفيفة والمحذوف نون الوقاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God gave Solomon is primarily prophethood and unexcelled sovereignty, compared with their wealth; taking it as material wealth is possible but less eloquent and less fitting.
rows.anchor: أي من النبوة والملك الذي لاغاية وراءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence explains the rejection indirectly: Solomon needs no gift and assigns it no value, rather than boasting about what he received.
rows.anchor: والكلام كناية عن عدم القبول لهديتهم وليس المراد منه الافتخار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sequence has Solomon say this as soon as the envoys arrive, perhaps from eagerness to guide them; another view places it after the exchanges reported by Wahb and others.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الخطاب المذكور كان أول ما جاؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports recommending the return of gifts from polytheists when doing so serves a religious interest, not as an unconditional rule.
rows.anchor: واستدل بالآية على استحباب رد هدايا المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He did not phrase the clause as “what God gave me is better than what He gave you” so it could serve as a circumstantial clause: a confirmatory state must be known, whereas this reason was not.
rows.anchor: وإنما لم يقل : وما آتاني الله خير مما آتاكم لتكون الجملة حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the clause as a shift from rejecting the gift to exposing the envoys' worldly outlook: they rejoice in gifts because their aspirations are confined to worldly increase.
rows.anchor: إلى بيان ما حملهم عليه من قياس حاله عليه السلام على حالهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading reproaches them for rejoicing in their gift to Solomon with pride, a sense of obligation, or self-regard; this makes their presumption in treating him as a great king especially blameworthy.
rows.anchor: إلى التوبيخ بفرحهم بهديتهم التي أهدوها إليه عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive construction can attribute the gift either to its recipient or to its giver.
rows.anchor: والهدية مضافة إلى المهدى إليه وهي تضاف إلى ذلك كما تضاف إلى المهدى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: They may rejoice because they expect a greater return, material or otherwise, from a gift to a ruler, such as preventing their lands from being destroyed.
rows.anchor: من حيث توقعهم به ما هو أزيد منه فان الهدايا للعظماء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A subtler view makes this a euphemistic refusal: they should take back the gift and rejoice in receiving it, since Solomon has no need of it; al-Ālūsī calls this reading obscure.
rows.anchor: أنتم من حقكم تفرحوا بأخذ الهدية لا أنا فخذوها وافرحوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording's indefinite “gift” may signal the queen's pride in the offering, recalling the earlier reports about the box, gem, and disguised attendants.
rows.anchor: وينبيء عن اعتدادهم بتلك الهدية التنكير في قول بلقيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening fāʾ is explicative of an omitted sequence: the mother nursed him and cast him into the river as commanded, with the deletion conveying how promptly she obeyed.
rows.anchor: والفاء في قوله تعالى : ( فالتقطه آل فرعون ( فصيحة والتقدير

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A midwife summoned at Moses' birth saw light between his eyes, felt her limbs tremble and love for him, and urged his mother to hide him; when Pharaoh's agents searched, his mother hid him in a blazing oven, where God made the fire cool and safe.
rows.anchor: لما ضربها الطلق دعت قابلة من الموكلات بحبالى بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: After nursing him for three, four, or eight months according to differing reports, his mother feared discovery and made a reed chest coated inside with pitch.
rows.anchor: وأرضعته ثلاثة أشهر أو أربعة أو ثمانية على اختلاف الروايات

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says she had a carpenter make a chest with its lock inside and set Moses in the Nile near Pharaoh's house; Asiya's bathing attendants found it, mistook it for treasure, and brought the child to her.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي أنها دعت نجارا فصنع لها تابوتا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Asiya loved Moses and persuaded Pharaoh to spare him when he wanted to kill him.
rows.anchor: وأراد فرعون قتله فلم تزل تكلمه حتى تركه لها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: A report says Pharaoh's only child, a daughter afflicted with severe leprosy, was told that the saliva of a human-like being found at the Nile on a certain sunrise would cure her; she rubbed Moses' saliva on her skin and recovered.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس وغيره أنه كان لفرعون يومئذ بنت

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One continuation says the girl was cured merely by seeing Moses' face; Pharaoh's advisers suspected he was the feared child, but Asiya asked Pharaoh to give him to her and he relented.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لما نظرت إلى وجهه برأت فقالت الغواة من قوم فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl Firʿawn means Pharaoh's followers; restricting āl to people of noble standing reflects the usual case, or a broader honor that includes both real and outward rank.
rows.anchor: وآل فرعون أتباعه وقولهم : إن الآل لايستعمل إلا فيما فيه شرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their taking him is like picking up a lost object: they deliberately cared for him and protected him from being lost.
rows.anchor: أخذ اللقطة أي أخذ اعتناء به وصيانة له عن الضياع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One analysis treats his becoming an enemy and grief as if it were the remote purpose of adoption and benefit, leaving the comparison implicit while the lām retains its literal purposive sense.
rows.anchor: الأول أن يشبه كونه كدوا وحزنا بالعلة الغائبة

rows.speaker: السكاكي والتفتازاني
rows.claim: Al-Sakkākī, followed by al-Taftāzānī, first compare the arrangement of non-final and final purposes, then use the lām metaphorically for the resulting arrangement; the trope is primary in causality and derivative in the particle.
rows.anchor: كما ذهب إليه السكاكي وتبعه العلامة التفتازاني

rows.speaker: الخطيب الدمشقي
rows.claim: Al-Khaṭīb al-Dimashqī's analysis first compares Moses' being their enemy and grief with a final purpose, then transfers that comparison to the relation expressed by the lām, without a trope in its genitive.
rows.anchor: ما أفاده كلام الخطيب الدمشقي في التلخيص والايضاح

rows.speaker: العلامة عبد الحكيم
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm calls al-Khaṭīb's analysis correct: since the lām's meaning depends on its genitive, its figurative transfer should follow the comparison applied to that genitive, not an abstract comparison of meanings.
rows.anchor: واختار ذلك العلامة عبد الحكيم فقال : وهو الحق عندي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that picking something up is involuntary and so cannot have a purpose is mistaken: the purpose belongs to their deliberate taking and care of what they found.
rows.anchor: واستشكل أصل تعليل الالتقاط بأن الالتقاط الوجدان من غير قصد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some attach the lām to an implied “He decreed the taking so that…,” but al-Ālūsī dismisses this as an unsuitable supposition about God's speech.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم يحتمل تعلق اللام بمقدار أي قدرنا الالتقاط ليكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Moses himself grief is an emphatic exaggeration.
rows.anchor: وفي جعله عليه السلام نفس الحزن مالا يخفى من المبالغة

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وابن سعدان
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn Saʿdān read ḥuznan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وابن سعدان حزنا بضم الحاء وسكون الزاي

rows.speaker: جمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ḥazanan with both the ḥāʾ and zāy bearing fatḥa; this is the language of Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الجمهور بفتحتين لغة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were wrong in all they did and left, or habitually erring; their killing thousands of infants and then raising Moses was no new departure from their error.
rows.anchor: في كل ما يأتون وما يذرون أو من شأنهم الخطأ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says ninety thousand newborn boys were slaughtered while Pharaoh's people searched for Moses.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه ذبح في طلبه عليه السلام تسعون ألف وليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāṭiʾīn may derive from error in judgment, or from khaṭiʾa, to sin deliberately; on the latter reading it means sinners, whom God punished by having their enemy raised in their own care.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون من خطيء بمعنى أذنب وفي الاساس يقال : خطيء خطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If it means error, the closing clause is parenthetical and reinforces the error already implied by the ironic claim that they raised an enemy and grief; if it means sin, it reinforces their guilt.
rows.anchor: والجملة على الأول اعتراض بين المتعاطفين لتأكيد خطئهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: On the sin interpretation, some say the clause must be parenthetical to explain the cause of their affliction; if that affliction means Moses becoming their enemy and grief, it may also be an explanatory resumption.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يتعين عليه أن تكون اعتراضا لبيان الموجب لما ابتلوا به

rows.speaker: قُرِئَ
rows.claim: A non-hamzated reading is most plausibly the same word with its hamza dropped; another suggestion derives it from khaṭā, to step, figuratively missing the right course.
rows.anchor: وقريء خاطئين بغير همز فاحتمل أن يكون أصله الهمز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṭsh means seizing or striking with force and dominance.
rows.anchor: والبطش الاخذ بصولة وسطوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ʿaduww intensifies the sense, marking formidable enmity; the wording is not put into a possessive construction.
rows.anchor: والتنوين في عدو للتفخيم أي عدو عظيم العداوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man Moses meant to strike was the Copt, since the Copts were especially hostile to the Israelites; another view says he was an enemy to both because he followed neither man's religion.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالذي هو عدو لهما القبطي وقد كان القبط أعظم الناس عداوة

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū Jaʿfar read yabṭishu with ḍamma on the ṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو جعفر ( يبطش ) بضم الطاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators say the Israelite man said this, supposing Moses meant to strike him rather than the Copt because Moses had called him misguided.
rows.anchor: قاله الإسرائيلي الذي يستصرخه على ما روي عن ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the Copt said it, inferring from Moses calling the Israelite misguided that the Israelite was the man who killed the Copt the previous day; al-Ālūsī says this is possible.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : قاله القبطي الذي هو عدو لهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Ḥasan's account, the Copt's enmity to the Israelite follows from oppressing him, and his disobedience to God makes him Moses' enemy; religious difference is another possible basis of enmity.
rows.anchor: بأن هذا الذي أراد عليه السلام أن يبطش به كان ظالما لمن استصرخه

words: إِن تُرِيدُ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ جَبَّارًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī warns that the Torah is disregarded where it contradicts the Qurʾān or sound Sunna; elsewhere, like other Israelite reports, it is neither affirmed nor denied, though it may corroborate some details.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن هذ التوراة لا يلتفت اليها فيما يكذب القرآن أو السنة الصحيحة

words: إِن تُرِيدُ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ جَبَّارًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah's Moses narrative differs from the Qurʾānic account through additions and omissions; here it omits the believer from Pharaoh's family who comes to advise Moses and lacks support for the accusation of tyranny.
rows.anchor: وهي فيما عدا ذلك كسائر أخبار بني إسرائيل لا تصدق ولا تكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jabbār is one who does whatever he wants by striking or killing without weighing outcomes; another gloss is an arrogant person who will not submit to God's command, with the word likened originally to a tall palm.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي يفعل كل ما يريد من الضرب والقتل ولا ينظر في العواقب

rows.speaker: الشعبي وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says whoever kills two people without right is a tyrant, citing this verse; Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports a similar statement from ʿIkrima.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن الشعبي أنه قال : من قتل رجلين أي بغير حق فهو جبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reformers are those who settle disputes among people by using the better course.
rows.anchor: بين الناس فتدفع التخاصم بالتي هي أحسن

words: وَمَا تُرِيدُ أَن تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After this accusation spread to Pharaoh and his chiefs, they resolved to kill Moses; a believer from Pharaoh's family, his cousin, came to warn and advise him, leading into the next verse.
rows.anchor: ولما قال هذا انتشر الحديث وارتقى إلى فرعون وملائه فهموا بقتل موسى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The man from the city's outskirts is variously named Shimʿān, Shimʿūn son of Isḥāq, Ḥizqīl, or another name.
rows.anchor: واسمه قيل : شمعان وقيل : شمعون بن إسحاق وقيل : حزقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known identification is that he was the believer from Pharaoh's family; another view identifies him as someone else.
rows.anchor: وكون هذا الرجل الجائي مؤمن آل فرعون هو المشهور وقيل هو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of yasʿā is that he hurried because he lived far away and was keen to warn and advise Moses.
rows.anchor: ويسعى بمعنى يسرع في المشي وإنما أسرع لبعد محله ومزيد اهتمامه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes yasʿā figuratively as seeking God's good pleasure, as in the wording of 17:19.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يسعى بمعنى يقصد وجه الله تعالى كما في قوله سبحانه : ( وسعى لها سعيها )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min aqṣā al-madīna most naturally modifies jāʾa; alternatively it describes the man, with yasʿā another adjective, or—with the phrase adjectival—yasʿā can be a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ( من أقصى ) صلة ( جاء ) وجملة ( يسعى ) صفة ( رجل )

rows.speaker: سيبويه والجمهور
rows.claim: If min aqṣā modifies jāʾa, most grammarians bar yasʿā as a circumstantial clause from the indefinite man; Sībawayh allows it because the prepositional phrase makes the noun definite-like.
rows.anchor: وأما إذا كان متعلقا بجاء فمنع ذلك الجمهور وأجازه سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attaching min aqṣā to yasʿā is also proposed, but al-Ālūsī dismisses it as implausible.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يعلق الجار والمجرور بيسعى وهو كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-malaʾ refers to the leading figures of Pharaoh's government.
rows.anchor: وهم وجوه أهل دولة فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʾtamirūna bika means they are consulting about you; the term reflects each adviser both ordering and complying with the others, and their plan is to kill Moses.
rows.anchor: أي يتشاورون بسببك وإنما سمي التشاور ائتمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in laka is clarifying and attaches to an omitted expression, like suqyā laka; most grammarians reject attachment to al-nāṣiḥīn because its al- is relative and the complement cannot precede it.
rows.anchor: اللام للبيان كما في سقيا لك فيتعلق بمحذوف

rows.speaker: بعض النحاة
rows.claim: Some grammarians allow laka to attach to al-nāṣiḥīn or to an implied term it explains, under analyses that permit advancing a complement before this al or treat it as a definite article.
rows.anchor: وعند من جوز تقدم معمول الصلة إذا كان الموصول أل خاصة

rows.speaker: القرطبي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī and others infer from the verse that informing on someone is permissible when it serves a religious interest.
rows.anchor: واستدل القرطبي وغيره بالآية على جواز النميمة لمصلحة دينية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses left the city in compliance with the warning.
rows.anchor: فخرج منها ( أي من المدينة ممتثلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He was afraid and watchful for pursuers to catch up with him.
rows.anchor: خائفا يترقب ( لحوق الطالبين
